summary: A draft design from SRI-ARC for a protocol covering both text and graphics, put together from existing ideas rather than new ones. The authors were concerned that the graphics protocol suggested in RFC 493 handled text poorly and would shape future graphics interfaces.

eli5.summary: People wanted one set of rules for sending both words and drawings between computers. This is a first draft that borrows the best ideas so far.

questions: what is the text graphics protocol
how do structured display files work
what is a call unit in graphics
subtitle: A unified protocol for text and graphics over the network

tldr.problem: Different computer systems lacked a common way to send both text and graphics over the network, and existing graphics proposals handled text poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a display protocol with two levels: segmented files for simple graphics and structured files with reusable graphics components, all embedded in telnet with special command markers.
tldr.outcome: The proposal identified key architectural ideas (primitives, subpictures, call units) but the encoding was incomplete and the protocol did not proceed to standardization.

today: RFC 553 is a historical draft specification. It did not proceed to standardization and the graphics protocol remained unresolved, with later work taking different directions.

sections.title: The Need for a Graphics and Text Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 553 addresses the problem that ARPANET hosts needed a common way to display both text and graphics over network connections. The authors were concerned that existing graphics protocols, particularly RFC 493, did not handle text well and would shape future network graphics interfaces in undesirable ways. Rather than proposing entirely new ideas, they synthesized existing work from multiple institutions (ARC, PARC, and BBN) into a draft specification.

The key insight was that the protocol should work within telnet by wrapping graphics commands between special BEGIN-GRAPHICS-COMMAND and END-GRAPHICS-COMMAND markers, allowing programs to use either pure text, pure graphics, or a mixture depending on need.
sections.eli5: The authors worried that if everyone used a bad graphics system, it would be hard to fix later. They took the best ideas from different places and put them together into one design that works with the regular remote-login tool.

sections.title: Two Levels of Display Files
sections.content:
The protocol defines two different ways to organize display information. Segmented display files are simple: named segments containing primitive units (strings, lines, dots) that display immediately when created or modified. This suits basic graphics applications. Structured display files are more powerful: they organize content as named subpictures containing both primitive units (drawing instructions) and call units (references to other subpictures). Call units can include transformations like scaling, rotation, and color control, enabling hierarchical, reusable graphics components.

Each host believes it has complete control of its own display file, though a terminal may actually be shared among multiple hosts. The protocol allows unescorted text characters to flow to a designated tty-unit, so the same connection can handle both graphics commands and live typing.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to organize drawings: simple mode just draws shapes directly, and fancy mode saves named drawings and can reuse them with different sizes, rotations, and colors. Both can handle typed text at the same time.

sections.title: Primitive and Call Units
sections.content:
Primitive units produce visible output: strings (horizontal text with positioning), dots, lines, special curves (using Flegal's spline algorithm), and device-specific commands. Each carries mode information such as blinking, intensity, and in the case of strings, embedded font and mode specification characters. TTY units simulate an alphanumeric display within a rectangle, handling line wrapping, scrolling, and control characters like carriage return and line feed.

Call units provide subroutine-like capability in structured files. A call unit names another subpicture and can apply transformations: master/instance rectangles for independent scaling and translation, rotation, and intensity/color control. This allows one drawing to be displayed multiple times with different appearance without storing duplicate geometry.
sections.eli5: Primitive units are the actual shapes you see: text, dots, lines, and curves. Call units are like naming a drawing and then showing it again somewhere else, maybe rotated or bigger. You do not have to draw it twice.

sections.title: Commands and Direct Feedback
sections.content:
The RFC defines editing commands for both segmented and structured display files. For segmented files, commands create, delete, or replace segments and their primitive units. For structured files, commands create or clear subpictures, create or modify units within them, delete units, control visibility, and apply visual modes. An UPDATE-STRUCTURED-DISPLAY command forces the display to reflect accumulated changes. Direct feedback features—dragging, tracking, inking, and rubber banding—are proposed as optional capabilities for smooth interaction without the delays of round-trip network commands.

The encoding scheme places commands between BEGIN and END graphics markers and uses 7-bit encoding with continuation bytes for numbers and 14-bit identifiers for subpictures and units. The RFC notes that the actual full encoding was deferred pending further design discussion.
sections.eli5: Commands create and change drawings. You can hide shapes, move them, or change their colors. Some cool features let the display respond instantly to your mouse without asking the server first. The exact encoding of all this was not finished yet.
